edits.notes:
On 2026-10-08 I opened every page behind a rewrite or a source change. Pages checked: connection-strings, enable-tag-inheritance, Cosmos DB integrated-cache, ADF managed-virtual-network-private-endpoint, Synapse on-demand-workspace-overview, ASR recovery-plan-overview, spot-vms, template-specs, CAF ready/landing-zone, dms-overview, storage-mover service-overview, App Service overview-private-endpoint, load-balancer cross-region-overview and virtual-wan-about. The 5 tell rewrites reuse sources the verifiers already confirmed and keep each card's fact and answer.

Main decisions:
(1) Weak cards are dropped by default. Five sections would have fallen below 4:6 (or below 9 cards) if all their weak cards went, so in those sections I rewrote the minimum number of cards using the verifier's replacement: 2.2-04, 2.3-03 and 2.3-08, 3.1-03, 4.1-01, 4.3-01. In 4.3 I chose the landing zone replacement over Data Box export, so 4.3-11 is dropped and the data-box-seeding conflict group goes away.
(2) 4.2-10 is rewritten, not dropped. The template-specs page still says "Users only need read access to the template spec to deploy its template". The new wording ("is enough ... to deploy its resources into a resource group") targets the documented extra need for ARM deployment permissions. I did not use the verifier's "with no rights" because it is a negation. If you want zero risk, drop it instead: 4.2 would then be 11 cards, 6T/5F.
(3) 4.3-12 (explanation_error) is rewritten onto the verifier's preferred Storage Mover single-instance fact, not the AzCopy minimum fix. The AzCopy card hinged on a CLI option default, which the prompt excludes. It was also the fourth false card on the preserve-on-copy template.
(4) 4.4-07 drops 'automatically' from the verifier's suggested statement, because 'automatically' on a false card is a tell.
(5) 4.4-04 changes only its source, to the Global load balancer page.

Tells: the strongest pattern was 'built-in/native' meaning false (6 of 7 cards). The 4.3-08 rewrite plus the tell rewrites of 4.2-04, 2.1-03, 2.2-09 and 1.2-11 bring it down to 1 false (2.3-12) against 1 true (2.1-01). The 2.3-06 tell rewrite removes 'uninterrupted' and breaks the mirrored 'Synapse lets X continue' template.

Remaining known issues:
- The preserve-on-copy false template still has 3 cards (1.1-04, 4.2-12, 4.3-09), one over the 2-per-template cap. They are kept in one conflict group. If you want strict compliance, a later pass should rephrase or replace one of them.
- 'Microsoft recommends' still leans true: 1.2-10 and 2.2-08 are true, 3.2-07 is false.
- Verifier side notes that I did not edit: 1.1-04 volatility could be may_change. 2.3-09's explanation could say "when periodic refresh is on". 2.3-10 difficulty looks mislabelled. 2.1-10 difficulty is probably 2. No card should claim Hyperscale has zero In-Memory OLTP support (the page now says Hyperscale supports a subset).
- The deck files are unchanged: this was a read-only pass, with no git and no subagents.

cards.statement: The instrumentation key in an Application Insights connection string acts as a security key against forged telemetry.
cards.explanation: The instrumentation key only identifies the Application Insights resource and isn't a security key. To reject unauthenticated telemetry, disable local authentication and require Microsoft Entra ID.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The connection-strings page says "Ikey unique identifiers aren't security tokens or security keys" and that disabling local authentication enforces Microsoft Entra ID.

cards.statement: Cost Management tag inheritance copies resource group tags onto the resources in the group.
cards.explanation: Tag inheritance applies subscription and resource group tags to child resource usage records, not to the resources themselves, so costs can be grouped without tagging every resource.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The enable-tag-inheritance note says "Inherited tags are applied to child resource usage records and not the resources themselves."

cards.statement: An Azure Cosmos DB read with Bounded staleness consistency skips the integrated cache and costs backend RUs.
cards.explanation: The integrated cache serves only Session and Eventual reads, at zero RU on a hit. Strong, Bounded staleness and Consistent prefix reads are served from the backend and use RUs.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The integrated-cache page says it supports session and eventual reads only, the other levels bypass it and are served from the backend, and cache hits cost zero RU.

cards.statement: A managed private endpoint in Azure Data Factory reaches a storage account only after the account's owner approves it.
cards.explanation: Creating a managed private endpoint opens a Pending private endpoint connection. The storage account owner approves or rejects it, and only an approved endpoint can send traffic.
cards.reason: Both lenses fixed the same problem: 'its owner' could mean the data factory side. The wording lens's statement is 125 characters, over the limit, so I used the fact lens's 118-character version. Checked on the ADF page (updated 2026-08-05): the connection starts as "Pending", "The private link resource owner is responsible for approving or rejecting the connection", and "Only a managed private endpoint in an approved state can send traffic".

cards.statement: Azure Synapse Analytics serverless SQL pool bills each query by the data it processes rather than by its run time.
cards.explanation: Serverless SQL pool reserves no resources and charges only for the data that queries process, which suits occasional exploration of data lake files.
cards.reason: Used the wording lens's statement, which sets 'data processed' against run time, a realistic alternative, instead of 'reserved compute', which follows from the word 'serverless'. I kept the editor's explanation and did not use the lens's new 'long but light query' claim, because the page does not state it and no lens checked it. Page: "There's no charge for resources reserved. You are only being charged for the data processed by queries you run". The exploration scenario is listed on the same page.

cards.statement: Azure Site Recovery fails over the machines inside one recovery plan group one at a time.
cards.explanation: Machines in one recovery plan group fail over in parallel. Order applies between groups: Group 2 machines start failing over only after every Group 1 machine has failed over and started.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The recovery-plan-overview page says "Machines in a single group fail over in parallel" and that Group 2 starts only after all Group 1 machines have failed over and started.

cards.statement: An Azure Spot Virtual Machine evicted under the Deallocate policy keeps incurring storage charges for its disks.
cards.explanation: Deallocate, the default eviction policy, stops the VM but keeps its disks, which stay billed while the VM counts against quota. The Delete policy removes the disks together with the VM.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The spot-vms page gives Deallocate as the default, says deallocated VMs count against quota and are charged for their disks, and says Delete removes the disks.

cards.statement: Read access to a template spec grants a release team the rights to create the spec's resources in a resource group.
cards.explanation: Read access lets a team use a template spec without being able to change it. Creating its resources also needs the permissions for deploying an ARM template at the target scope.
cards.reason: Both lenses agree that 'is enough to deploy' can still be read as True, because the page says "Users only need read access to the template spec to deploy its template". I took the wording lens's framing, which asks what the permission grants (rights to create resources). That avoids the fact lens's extra 'read-only rights on a resource group' clause, which comes close to a strawman. The statement is 115 characters. The explanation stays on the cited page: "users with the template spec reader role can deploy it. In addition, you also need the permissions for deploying an ARM template." deploy-cli confirms this needs write access on the resources plus Microsoft.Resources/deployments rights.

cards.statement: One Cloud Adoption Framework workload landing zone holds a workload's development, test and production environments.
cards.explanation: Each workload gets a single workload landing zone with all its environments, each made of one or more subscriptions that inherit the platform landing zone's guardrails.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it, citing the CAF landing zone page (updated 2026-10-01): "Each workload has a single workload landing zone ... such as development, test, and production." The fact lens suggests setting volatility to may_change because the page was rewritten recently.

cards.statement: Azure App Service evaluates an app's access restriction rules for traffic that arrives through a private endpoint.
cards.explanation: App Service sends traffic from a private endpoint straight to the app without evaluating access restriction rules; network security groups restrict traffic to private endpoints.
cards.reason: The fact lens's objection holds. overview-access-restrictions says that when publicNetworkAccess is null, "the default behavior is to enable access unless a private endpoint exists which changes the behavior to disable access". So by default, adding a private endpoint does block public traffic, and the rewrite's False answer could be defended as True. I used the fact lens's replacement. It is supported by "Access restrictions don't apply to traffic entering through a private endpoint" and "Restrictions to private endpoints are configured using network security groups" on that page, and by overview-private-endpoint (2026-09-17). Change the source to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/overview-access-restrictions (title 'App Service Access restrictions - Azure App Service'). New misconception: access restriction rules filter every inbound path to an App Service app, including private endpoints.
